title: Routing stitchboard: service map and ownership beads
content:
Purpose / context:
This is a working 'stitchboard' for how the pieces of the control plane should be split across teams and services for routing, multi-region failover, and runtime adapter coordination. Goal: surface crisp ownership while keeping operational handoffs minimal and failure modes explicit. This is an intentionally rough, share-first doc — use for design reviews and as a source for a formal ownership diagram later.

High-level constraints we must satisfy (recap):
- Route decision must be deterministic and explainable for audits and debugging.
- Runtime selection (model variant, quantized vs full precision) must be orthogonal to regional routing and capacity fallbacks.
- Minimal synchronous cross-region calls on the critical path for common requests (latency SLOs).
- Clear escalation paths and primary/secondary ownership for each decision surface.

Stitchboard metaphor: beads and threads
- Beads = coarse service boundary (API Gateway, Orchestrator, Adapter Catalog, Runtime Adapters, Routing Policy Store, Telemetry/Tracing).
- Threads = routing and control flows connecting beads (ingress -> policy -> selection -> dispatch -> fallback).
We assign ownership per bead and annotate the thread steward (who owns the policy code/config + runbooks).

Proposed bead ownership (short map):
- API Gateway (ingress, auth, TLS, rate-limit): owner = eng-api-gateway team (primary), eng-platform-engineering (secondary for platform behaviors).
- Routing Policy Store (policy truth, feature flags for routing): owner = eng-platform-engineering (primary), product-hosted-api (secondary for product rules).
- Orchestrator (canary, rollout, regional routing decision engine): owner = platform-orchestration subteam within eng-platform-engineering.
- Adapter Catalog (metadata about runtime adapters, compatibility matrix): owner = serving-runtime team (primary), applied-ml (secondary for model compatibility).
- Runtime Adapters (per-hardware adapters that do kernel selection, quantization toggles): owner = serving-runtime (primary), release-engineering (secondary for packaging).
- Regional Control Plane Proxy (lightweight regional control-plane to avoid cross-region chattiness): owner = platform-engineering infra (primary), site-reliability-engineering (secondary).
- Telemetry & Tracing (token-level cost attribution + route traces): owner = observability team (primary), eng-platform-engineering (secondary for route-level dashboards).

Notes on why these assignments:
- API Gateway: universal ingress concerns, auth, and customer-facing rate-limits. The gateway must not own model selection policy (keeps scope narrow).
- Routing Policy Store centralized in platform-engineering because policies need platform context (capacity, region-resources, tenant tier). Product rules (e.g., feature A -> use model X) are authored by product teams but stored in the policy store as namespaced entries; product teams get edit permissions scoped by namespace.
- Orchestrator owns rollout/canary and the authoritative selection logic that maps a policy + runtime capacity to a concrete adapter.
- Adapter Catalog belongs with serving-runtime since it includes technical compatibility (model layout, KV cache implications).
- Runtime Adapters must be tightly coupled to serving-runtime and have a clear CI/CD hand-off with release-engineering.

Routing decision flow (ideal fast path):
1) Client -> API Gateway: validate token, identify tenant and route metadata. Gateway enriches request with tenant metadata and a policy context header (opaque policy-bundle id).
2) Gateway calls local Regional Control Plane Proxy (fast, cached). The proxy fetches policy-bundle (from Routing Policy Store) if not cached.
3) Regional Proxy returns a routing hint: primary region, preferred adapter family, allowed fallbacks, and SLO targets.
4) Gateway forwards request (+ routing hint) to Orchestrator for final in-region adapter assignment. Orchestrator uses local capacity metrics and adapter catalog constraints to pick node(s).
5) Orchestrator returns adapter endpoint(s); Gateway streams request to the chosen runtime adapter (data plane).

Why the proxy: avoid synchronous cross-region reads on the gateway -> routing policy store for every request. Proxy caches policy-bundle and subscribes to policy updates. If proxy misses, it fetches with a bounded timeout and falls back to simple default policies.

Ownership table (policy surfaces) — each row is a single string (service | primary owner | secondary owner | SLAs/public runbook id):
- api-gateway | eng-api-gateway | eng-platform-engineering | RUNBOOK-APIGW-01
- routing-policy-store | eng-platform-engineering | product-hosted-api | RUNBOOK-POLICY-02
- orchestrator | eng-platform-orchestration | eng-platform-engineering | RUNBOOK-ORCH-03
- adapter-catalog | serving-runtime | applied-ml | RUNBOOK-ADCAT-04
- runtime-adapters | serving-runtime | release-engineering | RUNBOOK-RT-05
- regional-control-proxy | platform-infra | site-reliability-engineering | RUNBOOK-PROXY-06
- telemetry-route-traces | observability | eng-platform-engineering | RUNBOOK-OBS-07

Multi-region failure modes and who does what (short):
- Local capacity depletion in region A: Orchestrator performs intra-region bin-packing and if still saturated, consults Routing Policy Store for allowed remote regions; then it triggers the regional proxy to return cross-region hints. Primary owner: orchestrator (runbook ORCH-FAILOVER-01).
- Regional blackout (network partition): Regional Control Plane Proxy detects control-plane health loss (missing policy-store heartbeats) and flips to degraded mode: use last-known policy-bundle and prefer local cached adapters. Owner: platform-infra + SRE.
- Cross-region latency spike: Gateway + orchestrator incorporate RTT into routing decision; if expected tail latency > configured SLO, orchestrator prefers local lower-capacity adapter over remote high-capacity adapter to avoid tail amplification. Owner: eng-platform-engineering for policy tuning.

Boundaries and explicit handoffs (where we draw the line):
- Policy vs execution: Routing Policy Store contains declarative policies (e.g., "gold-tier -> prefer model X, allow remote fallback"), not bindings to specific hosts. Orchestrator binds policy to actual endpoints.
- Control plane state vs data plane calls: The control plane must never hold request payloads. All sensitive payloads must be sent directly from Gateway to runtime adapters over a separate authenticated channel.
- Catalog metadata vs runtime behavior: Adapter Catalog exposes capability flags (quantization safe, max sequence length). It should not be the service that mutates adapter runtime flags at request time — that is orchestrator's job via an adapter API.

Examples (decision scenarios):
- New model rollout for all gold-tier users in eu-west: Product creates a feature-flag entry in Routing Policy Store namespace product-hosted-api:gold-rollout-v2. Orchestrator picks 5% of traffic in region eu-west and uses adapter-catalog entry for model-v2 on quantized nodes. Ownership: product authors flag (policy store), orchestrator executes rollout, serving-runtime ensures adapter is available.
- Urgent region failover: SRE triggers routing-policy-store change to mark region as soft-avoid; orchestrator performs active re-route. The runbook must include communications (pager to product owners) and rollback steps.

Open questions / trade-offs we need to resolve in follow-ups:
- Policy granularity: tenant-level policy vs route-level policy. Recommendation: default to tenant-level with route-level overrides for critical routes. Need a small-scale perf test to measure policy-store read costs under tenant-level granularity.
- Sync vs async policy updates: proxies should subscribe to changes via streaming where possible to minimize stale policies. We must define TTL semantics for caches.
- Test harness: can we simulate multi-region capacity events in staging? Action item for release-engineering + SRE.

Action items / next steps:
- [Asha] Draft runbook templates for RUNBOOK-ORCH-03 and RUNBOOK-PROXY-06 (due 2026-02-20).
- [Marcus] Prototype Regional Control Plane Proxy with in-memory policy cache and subscription model (POC by 2026-03-01).
- [Ruth] Add policy-store namespacing and RBAC proposal to PLT-2891 (in PR now); include example tenant-policy YAML.
- [Diego] Work with serving-runtime to add adapter capability flags to catalog service (API & schema) and publish an initial compatibility matrix.

Runbook/operational notes (practical):
- Page flow for orchestrator failure: SRE -> Orchestrator on-call -> platform-orchestration lead -> serving-runtime on-call.
- Quick mitigation for bad policy push: routing-policy-store has a kill-switch (global "rollback to default" key) that platform-infra can flip. Test this every quarter.

Appendix A: tiny ascii bead map (bead:owner)
[API Gateway:eng-api-gateway]--(policy-bundle)->[Regional Proxy:platform-infra]--(bundle)->[Orchestrator:eng-platform-orchestration]--(catalog-lookup)->[Adapter Catalog:serving-runtime]--(dispatch)->[Runtime Adapter:serving-runtime]
Telemetry hooks: each arrow emits trace/span to observability.

Appendix B: Sample policy YAML (sketch)
---
namespace: tenant-acme
route: "chat.generate"
priority: gold
preferred_adapters: ["gpu-a100-quant", "cpu-int8"]
allow_remote_fallback: true
max_remote_rtt_ms: 1200
canary: {percent: 5, regions: [eu-west]}
---

Notes to reviewers: please annotate the bead map with concerns or disagreements inline in this doc (use Slack thread #platform-routing or comment on PLT-2891). We should align on policy-store API shape and proxy semantics before the prototype phase.

-- end stitchboard --
